categories.title: Data types
categories.description: Column type forms shown or described in the module.

entries.title: INT / INTEGER
notes: Stores whole numbers. INTEGER is an alias in MySQL/MariaDB.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: INT/INTEGER: Used for whole numbers.

entries.title: SMALLINT
notes: Use for smaller whole-number ranges.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: SMALLINT: Used for smaller whole numbers.
SMALLINT can store values like 32767 or -32768.

corrections.text: SMALLINT and INTEGER are not the same MySQL/MariaDB type: they use 2 and 4 bytes respectively.
corrections.label: MariaDB: data type storage

entries.title: TINYINT
notes: The module gives signed and unsigned ranges; the range depends on the dialect.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: TINYINT can hold integer values ranging from 0 to 255

entries.title: BIGINT
notes: Use for large whole numbers.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: BIGINT: Used for large whole numbers.

entries.title: DECIMAL / NUMERIC
entries.syntax:
column_name DECIMAL(precision, scale)
column_name NUMERIC(precision, scale)
notes: precision is total digits; scale is digits after the decimal point.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: DECIMAL(p, s)/NUMERIC(p, s): Used for fixed-point numbers

corrections.text: Page 43 incorrectly treats 999999.99 as outside NUMERIC(8,2). Six integer digits plus two fractional digits fit exactly.
corrections.label: MariaDB: DECIMAL

entries.title: FLOAT
notes: Approximate floating-point value; precision syntax is dialect-dependent.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: FLOAT: Used for single-precision floating-point numbers.

corrections.text: The PDF presents FLOAT mainly as a migration tool and ties precision to a 32-bit or 64-bit computer. FLOAT is an approximate numeric type.
corrections.label: MariaDB: FLOAT

entries.title: REAL
notes: Approximate floating-point value; its alias and precision depend on the SQL implementation.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: REAL: Another term for single-precision floating-point numbers.
REAL can store values similar to FLOAT.

corrections.text: The PDF calls REAL universally single precision. MariaDB’s default is DOUBLE; SQL mode can change the alias.
corrections.label: MariaDB: DOUBLE and REAL

entries.title: DOUBLE
notes: Approximate double-precision numeric type.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: DOUBLE: Used for double-precision floating-point numbers.

corrections.text: REAL may already be an alias of DOUBLE. Their relationship is not a universal “twice REAL” rule.
corrections.label: MariaDB: DOUBLE and REAL

entries.title: CHAR / CHARACTER
notes: Fixed-length character string. Omitted length defaults vary by dialect; MySQL/MariaDB use 1.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: CHARACTER or CHAR(n): Fixed-length character string
the default is set to one.

corrections.text: Padding spaces do not universally have “no effect,” as page 35 claims. Retrieval and comparison behavior depend on settings.
corrections.label: MySQL: CHAR and VARCHAR

entries.title: VARCHAR / CHARACTER VARYING
notes: The length is a maximum, not a minimum.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: CHARACTER VARYING or VARCHAR(n): Variable-length character string

corrections.text: VARCHAR(n) defines a maximum, not both a minimum and a maximum. A minimum needs another validation rule.
corrections.label: MariaDB: VARCHAR

entries.title: TEXT
notes: Large variable-length text; capacity and defaults depend on the DBMS.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: TEXT: Designed to store large blocks of variable-length text data.
TEXT can store long paragraphs or documents.

corrections.text: Page 35 gives the MySQL TEXT limit in characters. Its limit is bytes, so encoding affects the number of characters that fit.
corrections.label: MySQL: BLOB and TEXT

entries.title: MEDIUMTEXT
notes: Used by the PDF productlines example for larger text in MySQL/MariaDB.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: htmlDescription mediumtext

entries.title: BINARY
notes: Fixed-length binary string measured in bytes.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: BINARY(n): Fixed-length binary data.

entries.title: VARBINARY / BINARY VARYING
notes: VARBINARY is the MySQL/MariaDB form. The module also names BINARY VARYING; that spelling is dialect-dependent.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: BINARY VARYING or VARBINARY(n): Variable-length binary data.

corrections.text: Page 36 says a minimum and maximum can both be set. VARBINARY(n) sets only the maximum byte length.
corrections.label: MariaDB: VARBINARY

entries.title: BLOB
notes: Binary large object for files or other large binary values.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: BINARY LARGE OBJECT or BLOB
BLOB can store large binary files like an image file.

corrections.text: The PDF’s equality-only comparison and mandatory-locator transfer restrictions are not general MySQL/MariaDB BLOB rules.
corrections.label: MariaDB: BLOB

entries.title: MEDIUMBLOB
notes: Used by the PDF productlines example for larger binary data in MySQL/MariaDB.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: image mediumblob

entries.title: DATE
notes: Stores year, month, and day.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: DATE: Used for date values (year, month, day).
DATE can store values like '2023-07-06'.

corrections.text: The PDF’s lower bound of year 0001 is not MySQL/MariaDB’s documented normal DATE range.
corrections.label: MariaDB: DATE

entries.title: TIME
notes: MySQL/MariaDB precision is fractional-second digits (0–6). The module mixes dialects.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: TIME: Used for time values (hour, minute, second).

corrections.text: MySQL/MariaDB TIME(p) uses fractional-second precision from 0 to 6; it has no WITH/WITHOUT TIME ZONE modifier.
corrections.label: MariaDB: TIME

corrections.text: The valid PostgreSQL ordering is TIME(precision) WITHOUT TIME ZONE, not TIME WITHOUT TIME ZONE(precision). MySQL/MariaDB use TIME(precision).
corrections.label: PostgreSQL date/time types

entries.title: DATETIME
notes: Stores a calendar date and clock time.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: DATETIME: Used for date and time values.
DATETIME can store values like '2023-07-06 13:45:30'.

corrections.text: Page 39 mixes SQL Server’s older DATETIME starting year with microsecond precision. That is not a universal SQL DATETIME specification.
corrections.label: MariaDB: DATETIME

entries.title: TIMESTAMP
notes: Time-zone conversion and range depend on the DBMS. MariaDB does not store a time-zone identifier.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: TIMESTAMP: Used for date and time values, often with time zone information.

corrections.text: The PDF implies that TIMESTAMP retains time-zone information. MariaDB converts the value but stores no time-zone identifier.
corrections.label: MariaDB: TIMESTAMP

entries.title: YEAR
notes: Stores a year; supported ranges and two-digit behavior are dialect-specific.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: YEAR: Used for year values.
YEAR can store values like 2023.

corrections.text: The PDF’s two-digit mapping to 2000–2099 is inaccurate for MariaDB; historical mapping spans 1970–2069.
corrections.label: MariaDB: YEAR

entries.title: BOOLEAN / BOOL
notes: In MySQL/MariaDB, BOOLEAN and BOOL are aliases for TINYINT(1); the type alone does not restrict values to 0 and 1.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: BOOLEAN: Used for true/false values.

entries.title: ENUM
notes: Stores one value from a permitted list. Invalid-value handling depends on SQL mode.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: ENUM: Enumerated type, a string object with a value chosen from a list

corrections.text: Page 41 says every invalid value produces an error. Strict mode rejects it; non-strict mode can store a special empty-string error value with a warning.
corrections.label: MariaDB: ENUM

entries.title: SET
notes: MySQL/MariaDB type that stores a combination of permitted values.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: SET: Similar to ENUM, but can store multiple values
SET('red', 'green', 'blue')

entries.title: JSON
notes: Stores JSON-formatted data where supported; storage differs between MariaDB and MySQL.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: JSON types for storing structured data.

entries.title: Spatial types
notes: The PDF names spatial storage but does not specify a universal declaration or constructor. Use the target DBMS documentation.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: spatial data types for geographic information

entries.title: USE
notes: Selects the database for subsequent unqualified statements.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: USE Databasename

entries.title: SHOW DATABASES
notes: Lists databases visible to the connected account.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: SHOW DATABASES: Lists out the databases

entries.title: SHOW TABLES
notes: Lists tables in the selected database.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: SHOW TABLES: Shows the tables

entries.title: SHOW COLUMNS
notes: Shows column names, types, keys, nullability, and defaults.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: SHOW COLUMNS FROM tablename

entries.title: SHOW INDEX
notes: Shows indexes, including the primary key.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: SHOW INDEX FROM tablename

entries.title: SHOW TABLE STATUS
notes: The PDF prints SHOW TABLE standing; the valid MySQL/MariaDB form is SHOW TABLE STATUS.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: SHOW TABLE standing LIKE tablename

corrections.text: Page 45 prints “SHOW TABLE standing.” The actual MySQL/MariaDB command is SHOW TABLE STATUS.
corrections.label: MariaDB: SHOW TABLE STATUS

entries.title: DESCRIBE
notes: Displays a table's column definition details.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: DESCRIBE employees;

entries.title: CREATE DATABASE
notes: Select it afterward with USE.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: CREATE DATABASE database_name;

entries.title: CREATE TABLE
notes: Choose types from Data types. Separate column definitions with commas. Table-level keys go inside the parentheses.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: CREATE TABLE customers
Defines the columns of the table along with their data types and constraints
Creating a Table using MS Access
CREATE TABLE INHERITANCESQL

corrections.text: The page 59 table definition omits a comma after PropositionID INTEGER. Raw SQL is also validated by the database, contrary to the surrounding wording.
corrections.label: MariaDB: CREATE TABLE

entries.title: ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN
entries.syntax: ALTER TABLE table_name ADD COLUMN column_name data_type;

sourceEvidence.excerpt: ADD column_name datatype;

entries.title: ALTER TABLE ... DROP COLUMN
entries.syntax: ALTER TABLE table_name DROP COLUMN column_name;

sourceEvidence.excerpt: DROP COLUMN column_name;
DROP COLUMN phone_number;

entries.title: ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY COLUMN
entries.syntax: ALTER TABLE table_name MODIFY COLUMN column_name data_type [constraints];
notes: MODIFY COLUMN is the MySQL/MariaDB form; other systems use different syntax.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: MODIFY COLUMN column_name datatype;
MODIFY COLUMN email VARCHAR(150);

entries.title: Table comment
notes: Main template: MySQL/MariaDB. The PDF shows the PostgreSQL COMMENT ON form without naming its dialect.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: COMMENT ON TABLE table_name IS

corrections.text: COMMENT ON TABLE is a PostgreSQL form. MySQL/MariaDB use a table COMMENT option with CREATE TABLE or ALTER TABLE.
corrections.label: MariaDB table comments

sourceEvidence.excerpt: RENAME TABLE old_table_name TO

entries.title: TRUNCATE TABLE
notes: Removes all rows while retaining the table definition; transaction behavior is dialect-dependent.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: TRUNCATE TABLE table_name;

entries.title: DROP TABLE
notes: Removes the table and its data. Backups may be needed for recovery.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: DROP TABLE table_name;
DROP DATABASE my_database

corrections.text: The PDF says DROP is simply irreversible. Ordinary transaction rollback cannot undo it in MySQL/MariaDB, but backups may permit recovery; other systems have different DDL behavior.
corrections.label: MariaDB: implicit commits

entries.title: DROP DATABASE
notes: Removes the database and its objects. Confirm the target before running.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: DROP TABLE table_name;
DROP DATABASE my_database

corrections.text: The PDF says DROP is simply irreversible. Ordinary transaction rollback cannot undo it in MySQL/MariaDB, but backups may permit recovery; other systems have different DDL behavior.
corrections.label: MariaDB: implicit commits

entries.title: Column attributes
notes: Column-definition fragment. Use DEFAULT NULL only on a column that permits NULL.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: first_name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL
email VARCHAR(100) UNIQUE
textDescription varchar(4000) DEFAULT NULL
Productlines example includes VARCHAR DEFAULT NULL and a primary key.

entries.title: PRIMARY KEY
notes: Table-constraint fragments inside CREATE TABLE. A composite primary key is one key containing multiple columns.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: It is the unique identifier for each row in a table.

See the following orders and 
orderdetails tables:
sourceEvidence.visual: orders/orderdetails diagram: asterisks mark orderNumber and productCode in orderdetails

sourceEvidence.excerpt: Productlines example: PRIMARY KEY (productLine).
Orderdetails diagram shows orderNumber and productCode forming the composite key.

corrections.text: Page 15 says two rows have the same ID; primary-key duplicates are prohibited. The key’s position is not a requirement.
corrections.label: PostgreSQL: primary keys

entries.title: FOREIGN KEY
notes: Generalized table-constraint template for the named foreign-key relationship. Use inside CREATE TABLE after defining the columns; parent columns must form an eligible referenced key.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: A foreign key is a column or a set of columns

column productLine in the table 
products is called the foreign key column

corrections.text: The PDF describes only another table’s primary key and treats NULL as always allowed. The actual reference and nullability rules are broader.
corrections.label: PostgreSQL: foreign keys

entries.title: AUTO_INCREMENT primary-key column
notes: Column-definition fragment inside CREATE TABLE; use only one AUTO_INCREMENT column per table.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: employee_id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY

entries.title: INSERT INTO
notes: Without a column list, provide values for the table’s columns in their declared order. Prefer an explicit column list.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: INSERT INTO: Used to add new records (rows) into a table.
VALUES ('John', 'Doe', 'john.doe@example.com')

entries.title: UPDATE ... SET
notes: Without WHERE, every eligible row is updated.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: UPDATE: Used to modify existing records in a table.
If omitted, all rows in the table will be updated.

entries.title: DELETE FROM
notes: Without WHERE, every row is deleted while the table remains.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: DELETE: Use this assertion to erase remove one or more records

entries.title: SELECT
notes: select_list in other templates means columns, expressions, or *. FROM identifies the source table.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: SELECT: Used to retrieve data from one or more tables
SELECT * FROM customers;
the asterisks (*) retrieves all columns

a list of 
columns or expressions that you want to show in the result.

sourceEvidence.excerpt:
FROM 
members as m

entries.title: WHERE
entries.syntax: SELECT select_list FROM table_name WHERE search_condition;
notes: WHERE also restricts UPDATE and DELETE. It is evaluated before grouping in a filtered query.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: WHERE
The WHERE clause allows you to specify a search condition

entries.title: DISTINCT
entries.syntax: SELECT DISTINCT column1, column2 FROM table_name;
notes: Removes duplicate result rows; it does not delete source records.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: DISTINCT

sourceEvidence.excerpt: GROUP BY
using the INNER JOIN clause with the GROUP BY clause:

corrections.text: Page 93 describes total sales and shows a result but omits the query. This example is constructed from the diagram, not quoted from the PDF.

entries.title: HAVING
entries.syntax:
SELECT grouping_column, AVG(value_column)
FROM table_name
GROUP BY grouping_column
HAVING AVG(value_column) > threshold;
notes: Filters grouped results; WHERE filters input rows.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: HAVING

entries.title: ORDER BY
entries.syntax:
SELECT select_list FROM table_name
ORDER BY column1 [ASC|DESC], column2 [ASC|DESC];
notes: Each sort expression has its own direction; omitted direction defaults to ASC in common dialects.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: ORDER BY

only the order of values in the column2 
changes.

corrections.text: Page 72 says ORDER BY column1, column2 makes column2 descending. Both default to ascending; write DESC explicitly.
corrections.label: MariaDB ORDER BY

entries.title: LIMIT
entries.syntax: SELECT select_list FROM table_name LIMIT row_count;
notes: Supported by MySQL/MariaDB and some other systems.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: LIMIT

entries.title: Comparison operators
entries.syntax:
column_name = value
column_name != value
column_name > value
notes: Predicate fragments for WHERE or ON. The module explicitly shows =, !=, and >.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: standard comparison operators like = or !=
whose value in the jobTitle column is Sales Rep.

entries.title: BETWEEN
notes: Predicate fragment for WHERE; includes both boundaries.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: The BETWEEN operator returns TRUE if a value is in a range of values

entries.title: COALESCE / IFNULL
notes: Expression fragments for a SELECT list. COALESCE returns the first non-NULL value; IFNULL takes two arguments in MySQL/MariaDB.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: functions like COALESCE and IFNULL are used to provide default values

entries.title: LIKE
notes: Predicate fragment for WHERE. % matches zero or more characters; _ matches one character.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: The LIKE operator evaluates to TRUE if a value matches a specified pattern.

entries.title: AND, OR, and NOT
entries.syntax:
condition1 AND condition2
condition1 OR condition2
NOT (condition)
(condition1 OR condition2) AND condition3
notes: Predicate fragments for WHERE or ON. Parentheses make grouping explicit; AND has higher precedence than OR.

sourceEvidence.excerpt:
logical 
operator AND, OR and NOT.
The AND operator is a logical operator that combines two or more Boolean

returns true when 
either condition is true

MySQL always 
evaluates the OR operators after the AND operators.
WHERE (country = 'USA'

corrections.text: Page 78 says only one expression is true. SQL OR also returns TRUE when both conditions are true.
corrections.label: MariaDB logical OR

entries.title: NULL tests
entries.syntax:
column_name IS NULL
column_name IS NOT NULL
notes: Predicate fragments for WHERE. = NULL and != NULL do not test whether a value is missing.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: IS NULL and IS NOT NULL

entries.title: AVG — Aggregate function
notes: Expression fragment for a SELECT list or HAVING. The table’s AVG_FUNCTION placeholder is not a literal SQL function name.

corrections.text: The module uses AVG_FUNCTION as a placeholder. The actual average function is AVG(expression).
corrections.label: MariaDB AVG

sourceEvidence.excerpt: GROUP BY
Table 3.2 GROUP BY/HAVING syntax uses AVG_FUNCTION(column2).

categories.title: Joins
categories.description: Combine rows from related table sources.

entries.title: INNER JOIN
notes: Returns matching row combinations only.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: INNER JOIN - Combines rows from both tables only when there is a match
The INNER JOIN matches each row in one table with every row in other tables

entries.title: LEFT JOIN
notes: Keeps every left-table row; unmatched right columns are NULL.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: LEFT JOIN (or LEFT OUTER JOIN) - Returns all rows from the left table
the left join selects all data from the left table

entries.title: RIGHT JOIN
notes: Keeps every right-table row; unmatched left columns are NULL.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: RIGHT JOIN (or RIGHT OUTER JOIN) - Returns all rows from the right table
the column of the left table will have NULL in the final result set

corrections.text: Page 101 reverses the missing side. An unmatched RIGHT JOIN row keeps the right-table values; the left-table columns become NULL. Page 100 explains this correctly.
corrections.label: MariaDB JOIN syntax

entries.title: FULL OUTER JOIN
notes: This cross-dialect form is named in the module; it is not executable in MySQL/MariaDB. No workaround is added.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: FULL JOIN (or FULL OUTER JOIN)

corrections.text: The PDF prints native FULL JOIN beside MySQL examples. MySQL/MariaDB do not support that syntax directly.
corrections.label: MariaDB: JOIN syntax

corrections.text: FULL OUTER JOIN is supported by PostgreSQL; it is absent from native MySQL/MariaDB join syntax.
corrections.label: PostgreSQL joins

entries.title: CROSS JOIN
entries.syntax: SELECT select_list FROM left_table CROSS JOIN right_table;
notes: Returns the Cartesian product.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: CROSS JOIN - Returns the Cartesian product

entries.title: ON join condition
entries.syntax:
SELECT select_list
FROM left_table
INNER JOIN right_table ON left_table.column1 = right_table.column1
  AND left_table.column2 = right_table.column2;
notes: Generalized template for the module’s conditional join form; the predicates describe how rows match.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: The join condition specifies the rule for matching rows

entries.title: USING
notes: Use when both sources expose the same join-column name.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: you can use the USING clause

entries.title: Joining more than two tables
entries.syntax:
SELECT select_list
FROM first_table AS a
INNER JOIN second_table AS b ON a.key = b.key
INNER JOIN third_table AS c ON b.other_key = c.key;

sourceEvidence.excerpt: INNER JOIN t2 ON join_condition1

entries.title: Find unmatched rows
entries.syntax:
SELECT left_table.key
FROM left_table
LEFT JOIN right_table ON left_table.key = right_table.key
WHERE right_table.key IS NULL;

SELECT right_table.key
FROM left_table
RIGHT JOIN right_table ON left_table.key = right_table.key
WHERE left_table.key IS NULL;
notes: Test a joined key that cannot be NULL on a real matched row.

sourceEvidence.excerpt:
find rows in the left table that does not have 
corresponding rows in the right table.
find customers who have no order:
WHERE customerNumber is NULL

exclusions.reason: Kept in Lesson notes because it is a visual workflow, not SQL syntax.
The PDF names FULL JOIN but does not teach a workaround; no invented workaround is added.
The PDF names spatial types without specifying a declaration or constructor.
Named conceptually without a concrete declaration. Their definitions remain in Lesson notes; no CREATE TYPE syntax is invented.

exclusions.topic: Indexes, views and procedures as database objects
exclusions.reason: Mentioned as objects but not taught with their own creation/deletion syntax; no additional commands are introduced.

exclusions.topic: IN, UNION, COUNT, MIN, MAX and SUM templates
exclusions.reason: No named concrete instruction for these forms was found in the 105-page audit. General aggregate behavior and the total-sales example remain in Lesson notes; AVG corrects the AVG_FUNCTION placeholder.
JSON extraction, WKT constructors, referential actions and other advanced-lab extensions are outside this PDF syntax reference.
